 Photo by: Kendall Bulkiewicz / University of South Florida Athletics Keys to the Game: Bulls vs. Owls
 November 21, 2026 | Football
 Share: Joey Johnston / Athletics Senior Writer BOCA RATON — It looks like a shootout — again.
 When the South Florida Bulls (6-4, 2-4) face the Florida Atlantic Owls (6-4, 3-3) in Saturday afternoon's American Conference game, it's easy to visualize the teams combining to surpass 100 points and 1,000 total yards.
 Sound familiar?
 The Bulls just experienced a similarly wild affair, dropping a 52-41 home decision against the Memphis Tigers. Twelve minutes into the game, the Bulls trailed 21-0. They rallied furiously, actually taking a fourth-quarter lead, then surrendering it for good on a 76-yard touchdown on one of the dozen explosive plays (15 yards or greater) by Memphis.
 But here's where the story got really wild. South Florida had 13 explosive plays of its own, a season-high against a Football Bowl Subdivision opponent, showing a new-found ability to trade blows in an offensive showcase.
 Ninety-three combined points and and 1,133 yards.
 Which brings us to Saturday's challenge.
 FAU has the nation's 18th-best offense (450.5 yards per game) and the sixth-best passing attack (320.8 yards per game), while averaging 38.3 points (12th nationally).
 Can the Bulls force a punt or two, maybe mixing in a takeaway? That might be enough to decide the game.
 The bigger question: After rolling up 552 yards against Memphis (502 over the final three quarters), is there a new template for South Florida's offense? After all, the Bulls had averaged just 279.4 yards in the eight other games against FBS opponents.
 The Owls haven't put up much resistance this season with the nation's 136th-ranked defense (466.4 yards per game), which allows an average of 35.3 points.
 Statistics can lie, of course, but this has all the makings of a big-time shootout, a four-hour marathon.
 Here are the keys for South Florida to prevail:
 1. Let Luke Do His Thing 
Quarterback Luke Kromenhoek has started the past two games and played most of another after the injury to Michael Van Buren. Kromenhoek has provided juice, hope and some entertainment as well. Suddenly, South Florida's offense has become fun to watch.
 Kromenhoek hasn't been perfect, but his relentless effort has provided a spark. Against Memphis, Kromenhoek accounted for 417 yards with 22-for-37 passing for 271 yards, while rushing for 146 yards.
 "We showed great resolve (against Memphis) and it started with our quarterback (Kromenhoek) just playing gutsy,'' offensive coordinator Tim Beck said. "I love the way he plays. It's one of the reasons we were attracted to him and tried to get him here.
 "He reminds me a lot of guys I've had like J.T. Barrett (Ohio State) and Sam Ehlinger (Texas). That type of player. They find a way. It's not always pretty. But he (Kromenhoek) has great resolve and great toughness. He starts to embody what we are offensively and our culture. Our guys have gravitated to it for sure.''
 2. Start Fast 
The Bulls can't afford to fall behind 21-0 in the first quarter again. They failed to score a first-quarter touchdown in six of the nine games against FBS competition.
 This has been a recurring theme.
 3. Get After Veltkamp 
Owls QB Caden Veltkamp is a problem. He has a 69.2-percent completion rate with 3,086 yards, 29 touchdowns and six interceptions. WRs Easton Messer (86 catches for 1,033 yards and 13 touchdowns) and Kelby Valsin (76 catches for 923 yards and seven scores) are quality targets.
 "I think the quarterback (Veltkamp) and the receivers have an amazing connection,'' Bulls LB Zavier Hamilton said. "It's almost like they understand each other while they're running the routes.''
 It's up-tempo, quick-rhythm, almost a West Coast offense kind of feel.
 The Bulls must get Veltkamp off his rhythm and apply pressure. He can't be comfortable. If he has time to throw, it's lights-out. FAU has allowed just 19 sacks in 10 games, so it's not the easiest task. Whether it's the defensive linemen, the linebackers or the secondary, the Bulls have got to send waves of pressure.
 "They did a really good job of retaining their players and your chances for success go way up (with that),'' defensive coordinator Josh Aldridge said. "They've done a great job of building camaraderie. You can tell they run their system really well. Everybody is very confident in the timing and where they need to be. That's what stands out to me.
 "The ball comes out of the quarterback's hands at the right time. He throws the ball before he (receiver) is actually open. So you've got to pick your punches (on applying pressure). You've got to have the awareness of how you want to mix that in and change up the looks on him. We've got to be able to do the things we do already and just execute at a high level.''
 4. Play Keep Away 
Against Memphis, the Bulls had possession for 37 minutes, 55 seconds. That was the program's highest time of possession in five years (44:35 against Temple on Oct. 23, 2021).
 Under former head coach Alex Golesh, South Florida's up-tempo, high-octane offense scored quickly. So time of possession was not a relevant statistic very often.
 Saturday afternoon at FAU, South Florida's time of possession is a highly relevant statistic.
 Veltkamp and FAU's offense can't do damage if they don't possess the ball. So it's incumbent on South Florida's offense to keep the chains moving and be effective on the ground. The Owls are vulnerable against the run, ranking 137th (next to last) in the FBS by allowing 238 rushing yards per game (and a 6.03-yard average).
 Kromenhoek could have a big day on the ground. Also look for RB Jason Collins Jr. , who had a breakout game against Memphis (108 yards rushing, a 75-yard touchdown, three catches for 65 yards) and revitalized WR Mudia Reuben (six catches for 98 yards, two touchdowns against Memphis) in a high-percentage passing game.
 Joey Johnston
 Athletics Senior Writer
